newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian report says rights violations worsening.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian report says rights violations worsening.

text.p: Nigeria's human rights situation is deteriorating and without democracy Nigerians will not fully enjoy fundamental rights, a rights group said on Sunday.

"Our country is in the throes of socio-economic crisis...the press is repressed; the judicial system has been decimated; many professional bodies have been decapitated while others are being viciously disrupted," said the Committee for the Defence of Human Rights (CDHR), a Nigerian group opposed to the military government.
In an annual report for 1995 released in Lagos, the group said there was a "rise in the tide of violations in the year".
Nigeria caused international outrage last year when nine minority activists including Ken Saro-Wiwa were hanged for murder in defiance of worldwide appeals for clemency.
CDHR said that two areas of rights violations stood out -- "the treatment of the opposition or perceived opposition and the murder of the 'Ogoni Nine'."

Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation with 100 million people, plunged into turmoil in 1993 when the army annulled a presidential vote presumed to have been won by Moshood Abiola, a wealthy businessman.
He has been detained since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of military ruler General Sani Abacha, who had seized power in the mayhem that followed the annulment.

"While the regime throughout the year held on to Moshood Abiola, the labour leaders and other opposition figures arrested in the middle of 1994, it went ahead to arrest and detain more human rights activists during the year," the CDHR said.
A CDHR spokesman said: "The human rights situation in Nigeria has not changed from what it was last year."
The government maintains there are no political prisoners and that those detained are held for specific offences.
Many opposition men held after pro-Abiola riots and strikes in 1994 remain in jail while many others fled abroad.

In 1995, 40 alleged coup plotters were jailed, among them former army ruler Olusegun Obasanjo and his then deputy Musa Yar'Adua, as well as former CDHR president Beko Ransome-Kuti and four journalists.

But by far the most serious problem for Nigeria was the hanging last November of the Ogoni activists, which promptly earned Nigeria sanctions from the West and suspension from the Commonwealth, the club of Britain and its former colonies.

Last April, a United Nations team which visited to investigate the execution of Saro-Wiwa recommended setting up a human rights commission, which the government accepted. The body sat for the first time two weeks ago.
But CDHR said the world should "regard military rule as a crime against humanity and adopt measures to help stop the further commission of this crime against the Nigerian people".
Nigeria has been under military rule for most the time since independence in 1960.
Abacha, the seventh army ruler, is implementing a programme of phased elections he says will lead to full democracy in October 1998, but his critics dismiss this as a ruse.

"Insofar as Nigeria remains under the jackboot of military autocracy, our people will not be able to enjoy the basic rights and fundamental freedoms they are entitled to enjoy under a representative and accountable government," CDHR's report said.
